transcription: My son gave me a journal. I cried. He got commission. Today my 17-year-old son gave me a leather journal for my birthday. I teared up. It was thoughtful. Personal. Uncharacteristically heartfelt. Then he padded my shoulder and said, glad you liked it. I get 15% commission on premium bundles. Let's rewind. I own a bookstore. Or I did. Technically, I now own 51% of a bookstore. He owns the rest. And he earned it. It started small he wanted a summer job. I gave him one. Thought I'd teach him work ethic. Sweep the floors. Restock bookmarks. Maybe develop a mild hatred of the public. Instead, he became the most effective salesperson in the known retail universe. He doesn't sell. He disarms. You come in for a Sudoku book and leave emotionally raw with a bag full of poetry, herbal tea guides, and a journal you'll weep into nightly. He doesn't upsell. He sees into your soul and gently nudges it toward the hardcover section. He once sold a grieving man a gratitude journal using only the phrase, sometimes it helps to write to the version of them that still listens. I almost passed out behind the register. We had to start tracking his individual revenue because he was outperforming the rest of the staff combined. Eventually, I offered him commission just to slow him down. It didn't. So I offered equity. I was bluffing. He wasn't. He brought spreadsheets. A PowerPoint. He countered every clause in my offer. He wore a suit. I blinked, and he owned 49% of the business and renamed our loyalty program chapter two. Back to today. He gave me the journal. Said a stranger helped him pick it out. Told me he'd been holding the world's okayest ad mug before she suggested something better. I asked him if it was real. He smirked. Turns out, he placed the mug there. Time the encounter. Shows the moment. He engineered the entire thing. An emotional ambush disguised as fatherly healing. I-
